title: The luminous mind
hookLine: the mind is luminous, stained by passing visitors (AN 1.51)

lines: FROST AND DUST ON THE WINDOW.
THE LIGHT WAS THERE ALL ALONG.
cards: A window in winter. Frost on the glass, a smear from someone's hand, dust from the street. From inside, the day looks gray and blurred.
Then someone wipes it, the light comes straight through, and you realize the light was there the whole time. It was the glass that changed.
The Book of Ones, in the Numbered Sayings, has a pair of sentences that sound a lot like that window. They're only a few lines long, and Buddhist thinkers keep coming back to them.

teach.b: Here is the passage, paraphrased. Luminous, monks, is this mind.
And it is stained by defilements that arrive from outside. The untaught person doesn't understand this as it really is, so for them there is no developing of the mind. Then the pair.
Luminous, monks, is this mind. And it is freed from defilements that arrive from outside. The well-taught disciple understands this as it really is, so for them there is developing of the mind.

The Pali word for luminous is pabhassara: bright, shining, radiant. The word for the stains is agantuka: arriving, visiting, the word for a guest. Greed, anger, confusion: in this passage they're visitors.
They're not the house. That's the hopeful heart of it. If the stains were built into the mind, training couldn't help.
Because they arrive, they can leave, and the mind can be developed.
Buddhist traditions read the passage differently, and it's worth naming who says what.
Theravada commentators often explain the luminous mind as the mind in its resting state between active moments, not a hidden perfect self.
Some Mahayana teachers connect it with buddha-nature, the potential for awakening present in all beings. Some modern scholars point out that the Pali text says very little more than these few lines.
On the practical part, the passage is plain. The stains are guests. Guests can be shown the door.

how: Meditators in many Buddhist traditions practice noticing moods and defilements as passing visitors, and some, especially in Mahayana and Vajrayana schools, are taught to recognize the clear, knowing nature of mind itself.

clouded, dim and hard to see

games.q: the luminous mind: tap the pairs.

s: the passage says the stains are part of the mind's nature
it calls them agantuka, arriving visitors, which is why they can leave.
all Buddhist schools read the luminous mind the same way
Theravada commentators, Mahayana teachers and modern scholars read it differently.
the passage is in the Book of Ones
the first book of the Numbered Sayings, teachings about one thing.

games.q: the passage says the mind is luminous, stained by visitors. what does that mean for training the mind?
o: training is pointless, the stains are permanent.
because the stains arrive, they can leave, so the mind can be developed.
the mind is already perfect, so nothing needs doing.
games.why: the passage links understanding this to developing the mind: guests can go, so training helps.

practice: Notice the mood you're in right now and name it plainly, tired, irritated, flat, anxious, cheerful, then treat it as the passage does, as a guest that came in at some point today.
Without pushing it out, look past it, the way you'd look through a smeared window at the light behind. What's there underneath? Maybe just awareness, quiet, noticing; rest there.

wordCard.voice: Pabhassara. The Pali word for luminous or radiant, used in the Book of Ones for the mind, stained by defilements that arrive like visitors, and freed when they go. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali pabhassara: luminous, radiant, shining, used of the mind in AN 1.51–52.
